headline: HSC, equivalent exam results to be published on October 29
summary: The Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee officially announced the date, with more details regarding the publication process expected through a press release on October 26.
details: The results for this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations are scheduled for publication on October 29. This crucial announcement affects over 1.2 million candidates across Bangladesh.

The Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee confirmed the date in a notice issued recently. The notice was signed by committee president Prof Syed Akhtaruzzaman, who is also the chairman of the Dhaka Education Board.
Further details regarding the result publication process will be provided through a press release on October 26. Students and guardians are advised to look out for this official announcement.
A total of 12,70,583 candidates were registered under 11 education boards for this year’s examinations. The written tests commenced on July 2.
While written examinations concluded on August 8 for most boards, some tests under the Chattogram Education Board were delayed due to flooding. These postponed exams continued until September 9.

headline_marked: [[Hundreds of thousands protest across France]] over cost of living and education crisis; clashes reported
headline: Hundreds of thousands protest across France over cost of living and education crisis; clashes reported
summary: Millions took to the streets nationwide, with official figures reporting 410,000 participants and unions claiming nearly 800,000. Major cultural institutions like the Louvre were closed due to the demonstrations.
details: Hundreds of thousands of people marched across France on Saturday to protest the rising cost of living and the education system crisis. Official figures from the Interior Ministry reported 410,000 participants nationwide, while unions claimed the number was closer to 800,000.

One French mother, Emily Grandry, told Reuters she had to return to the streets despite facing tear gas in a previous protest, to protect her child's future. Her 15-year-old son Aaron highlighted dilapidated school buildings and a severe teacher shortage as key concerns.

Student Clara Lebbadi expressed frustration to Reuters, noting that people mourn broken shops but ignore those who become poorer throughout the year. A protest placard echoed this sentiment, asking, 'Those who break things get imprisoned. But what about those who hurt people?'

Protesters like student Laou and communications worker Nadege emphasized that stopping the movement out of fear would not achieve their demands. Teachers and retirees also joined, bringing their children and grandchildren, hoping for a better future.

The protests led to the closure of major cultural sites, including the Louvre Museum, Musée d'Orsay, and Paris Opera, preventing visitors from seeing world-famous artworks like the Mona Lisa. To control the situation, 70,000 police officers were deployed nationwide.
Clashes between police and protesters were reported on Saturday night in Paris and Marseille, highlighting the tension surrounding the demonstrations.
caption:
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across France on Saturday, protesting the rising cost of living and a crisis in the education system.

Hundreds of thousands of people marched across France on Saturday to protest the rising cost of living and the education system crisis. Official figures from the Interior Ministry reported 410,000 participants nationwide, while unions claimed the number was closer to 800,000.

One French mother, Emily Grandry, told Reuters she had to return to the streets despite facing tear gas in a previous protest, to protect her child's future. Her 15-year-old son Aaron highlighted dilapidated school buildings and a severe teacher shortage as key concerns.

Student Clara Lebbadi expressed frustration to Reuters, noting that people mourn broken shops but ignore those who become poorer throughout the year. A protest placard echoed this sentiment, asking, 'Those who break things get imprisoned. But what about those who hurt people?'

Protesters like student Laou and communications worker Nadege emphasized that stopping the movement out of fear would not achieve their demands. Teachers and retirees also joined, bringing their children and grandchildren, hoping for a better future.

The protests led to the closure of major cultural sites, including the Louvre Museum, Musée d'Orsay, and Paris Opera, preventing visitors from seeing world-famous artworks like the Mona Lisa. To control the situation, 70,000 police officers were deployed nationwide.

Clashes between police and protesters were reported on Saturday night in Paris and Marseille, highlighting the tension surrounding the demonstrations.
